title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
description: Brute force to optimized: extracting values and re-sorting from scratch versus splicing existing nodes directly with a dummy head.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Given the heads of two sorted linked lists l1 and l2, merge them into one sorted list by splicing together the nodes of the two original lists, and return the head of the merged list.

blocks.caption: A dummy head lets the smaller current node be spliced in directly at every step

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","The heads of two sorted (ascending) singly linked lists, l1 and l2"],["Output","The head of a single sorted linked list, formed by splicing together the nodes of l1 and l2 (not creating new nodes)"],["Goal","Merge in a single pass, reusing the existing nodes rather than extracting values and rebuilding"],["Constraints","The number of nodes in both lists is in the range [0, 50]; -100 <= Node.val <= 100; both l1 and l2 are sorted in non-decreasing order"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Merging two ALREADY-SORTED sequences into one sorted sequence","The classic two-pointer merge step from merge sort"],["The result should splice together EXISTING nodes, not create new ones","Directly re-link the smaller current node from whichever list into the result, advancing that list's pointer"],["Building a list where the very first node needs the same handling as every later node","Use a dummy (placeholder) head node to avoid special-casing the first real node"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given two sorted linked lists, merge them into a single sorted list by re-linking the existing nodes (not creating new ones), and return the head of the result.

blocks.title: Analogy: Interleaving Two Sorted Decks of Cards
blocks.text: Like merging two decks of playing cards, each already sorted in ascending order, into one single sorted deck, by always taking whichever card is currently on top of the two decks (the smaller one) and placing it face down onto a growing new pile, until one deck runs out, at which point the rest of the other deck is simply placed on top as-is.

blocks.caption: The smaller current node is spliced in at every step, then whichever list remains is attached at the end

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Compare 1 (l1) and 1 (l2): take l1's 1 (using <=, ties favor l1). Compare 2 (l1) and 1 (l2): take l2's 1. Compare 2 (l1) and 3 (l2): take l1's 2. Compare 4 (l1) and 3 (l2): take l2's 3. Compare 4 (l1) and 4 (l2): take l1's 4. l1 is now empty; attach the remainder of l2 (just [4])","Merged: [1,1,2,3,4,4]","Every comparison correctly picks the smaller of the two current nodes"],["Answer","[1,1,2,3,4,4]","This is the fully merged, sorted list"]]}

blocks.text: Edge case: one or both lists are empty
If either list is empty, the merged result is simply the other list unchanged (or an empty list, if both are empty).
5. How Should We Think?
Before extracting every value into a plain array and re-sorting from scratch, notice that both lists are ALREADY sorted, meaning a single coordinated pass can merge them directly.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Since both l1 and l2 are already sorted, the smallest remaining value overall must be either l1's current node or l2's current node, whichever is smaller.

Observation 2: Repeatedly picking the smaller of the two current nodes, splicing it directly into the result, and advancing that list's pointer, builds the merged list in the correct order using only the EXISTING nodes, never creating new ones.

Observation 3: Once one list is fully exhausted, the ENTIRE remainder of the other list is already sorted and can simply be attached as-is, with no further comparisons needed.

Observation 4: Using a dummy placeholder head node avoids needing special-case logic for attaching the very first node of the result, since every node (including the first) can be attached the exact same way, via dummy's "next" chain.

Recognizing that "merge two sorted sequences" only ever needs to compare the two CURRENT front elements at each step, never re-examining anything already placed, is what makes a single linear pass sufficient.
This is the classic two-pointer sorted-merge technique from merge sort's merge step, adapted to splice together existing linked list nodes directly, using a dummy head to simplify the code.
6. Brute Force Solution
Extract every value from both lists into a plain array, sort it from scratch, then rebuild an entirely new linked list from the sorted values.
Step by step algorithm

items: Walk through both l1 and l2, collecting every node's value into a single array.
Sort the combined array, then build a brand new linked list from the sorted values.

codes.python:
def merge_two_lists(l1, l2):
    values = []
    node = l1
    while node:
        values.append(node.val)                                            # collect every value from both lists into a plain array
        node = node.next
    node = l2
    while node:
        values.append(node.val)
        node = node.next
    values.sort()                                                          # sort the combined values from scratch
    dummy = ListNode(0)
    cur = dummy
    for v in values:
        cur.next = ListNode(v)                                             # rebuild a brand new linked list from the sorted values
        cur = cur.next
    return dummy.next


if __name__ == "__main__":
    l1 = ListNode(1, ListNode(2, ListNode(4)))
    l2 = ListNode(1, ListNode(3, ListNode(4)))
    result = merge_two_lists(l1, l2)
    values = []
    while result:
        values.append(result.val)
        result = result.next
    print(values)

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every value is collected first, since sorting requires having the full combined set of values available at once.
A brand new linked list is built from the sorted values, since this brute force does not reuse any of the original nodes.
The dummy head simplifies building the new list, avoiding special-case logic for the first node.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every value is collected and correctly sorted, so the resulting list is always accurate.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O((m+n) log(m+n)), dominated by sorting the combined array of m+n values.
Space: O(m+n), for the intermediate array and the entirely new set of nodes created.

Limitation: re-sorting the combined values from scratch, and creating brand new nodes, ignores that both input lists are ALREADY sorted, and that the existing nodes can simply be re-linked directly in a single linear merge pass.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force re-sorts everything from scratch. Instead, since both lists are already sorted, maintain a dummy head and a "current" tail pointer for the result. At each step, compare l1's and l2's current nodes, splice the smaller one directly into the result (reusing the existing node, not creating a new one), and advance that list's pointer. Once one list is exhausted, attach the entire remainder of the other list directly, since it's already sorted.

Create a dummy node and a cur pointer starting at dummy. While both l1 and l2 have remaining nodes, compare their current values, splice the smaller one's node into cur.next, and advance that list's pointer and cur. Once the loop ends (one list is exhausted), attach whichever list still has remaining nodes directly to cur.next. Return dummy.next as the head of the merged list.
9. Optimized Solution
Splice the smaller current node from l1 or l2 directly into the result at each step, using a dummy head to simplify the logic.

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: The merged list [1,1,2,3,4,4] matches the expected result.

codes.python:
def merge_two_lists(l1, l2):
    dummy = ListNode(0)                                                     # a placeholder head, avoiding special-casing the very first node
    cur = dummy
    while l1 and l2:
        if l1.val <= l2.val:
            cur.next = l1                                                  # splice the smaller current node directly into the result
            l1 = l1.next
        else:
            cur.next = l2
            l2 = l2.next
        cur = cur.next
    cur.next = l1 if l1 else l2                                            # attach whichever list still has remaining nodes
    return dummy.next


if __name__ == "__main__":
    l1 = ListNode(1, ListNode(2, ListNode(4)))
    l2 = ListNode(1, ListNode(3, ListNode(4)))
    result = merge_two_lists(l1, l2)
    values = []
    while result:
        values.append(result.val)
        result = result.next
    print(values)

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(m + n), a single pass through both lists combined.
Space: O(1) extra, reusing the existing nodes rather than creating new ones (excluding the space for the dummy node itself).
Why This Works

Because both l1 and l2 are already individually sorted, the overall smallest remaining value at any point must be one of their two current front nodes; picking the smaller one and advancing only that list's pointer preserves the correct sorted order in the result. Once one list is fully exhausted, the other list's remaining nodes are already sorted relative to everything placed so far (since every value already placed is <= every remaining value in the still-active list), so they can be attached directly without further comparisons.

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: dummy is a placeholder node whose value is never used; only dummy.next (the true head of the merged list) matters at the end.
cur always points to the last node successfully spliced into the result, ready to receive the next one via cur.next.
The final cur.next = l1 if l1 else l2 handles attaching the remaining list in a single line, without needing an additional loop.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Merging two already-sorted sequences never requires re-sorting from scratch; a single coordinated pass, always advancing whichever sequence contributed the smaller element, is both correct and optimal, and a dummy head node is a broadly useful trick for simplifying linked list construction.
Common mistakes

items: Extracting values and rebuilding a new list instead of splicing the existing nodes directly, wasting both time and space.
Forgetting to attach the remaining (non-empty) list once the other one is exhausted, silently dropping its nodes from the result.
Not using a dummy head, forcing awkward special-case logic to determine and set the correct first node of the result.

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Mention the dummy head technique explicitly as a general-purpose linked list construction simplification, since it's broadly reusable far beyond just this specific problem.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Merge two ALREADY SORTED lists/arrays" points toward the classic two-pointer merge technique (as in merge sort's merge step), never requiring a full re-sort.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you extend this to merge k sorted lists, not just 2? This becomes Merge k Sorted Lists, typically solved with a min-heap or by repeatedly merging pairs of lists (divide and conquer).

How would you merge them recursively instead of iteratively? Compare the two current heads, recursively merge the rest, and attach the result to whichever head was smaller; this is elegant but uses O(m+n) recursion stack space instead of O(1).
What if the lists were sorted in DESCENDING order instead? Simply flip the comparison operator (>= instead of <=) to pick the larger current node first.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: The classic sorted-merge technique from merge sort, adapted to linked lists via node-splicing rather than array writes; directly extended in Merge k Sorted Lists and reused as a subroutine in Sort List elsewhere in this category.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O((m+n) log(m+n)) time, O(m+n) space.
Optimized (splice smaller node directly): O(m + n) time, O(1) extra space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Two-pointer sorted merge, splicing existing nodes directly using a dummy head
Core Idea: At each step, splice in whichever of l1's or l2's current node is smaller; once one list empties, attach the other's remainder directly
Time: O(m + n)
Space: O(1) extra
Most Important Observation: Merging two already-sorted sequences only ever requires comparing their two current front elements, never re-sorting from scratch
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: Dummy head; splice the smaller of l1/l2 each step; attach the leftover list at the end
